11. In support of his contentions, the learned counsel for petitioner has relied on the following judgments:
(1) In Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels and Tours Pvt. Ltd.1, wherein, it is held:
(2012) 5 SCC 661 GAC, J "The core issue that has emerged in these two appeals is whether the company could have been made liable for prosecution without being impleaded as an accused and whether the directors could have been prosecuted for offences punishable under the aforesaid provisions without the company being arrayed as an accused.
Being aggrieved by the said order, she invoked the jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing of the criminal proceeding and the High Court,
considering the scope of Sections 138 and 139 of the Act and various other factors, opined that the ground urged would be in the sphere of defence of the accused and would not strengthen the edifice for quashing of the proceeding."

entities.text: Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels and Tours Pvt. Ltd.1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Applying the doctrine of strict construction, we are of the considered opinion that commission of offence by the company is an express condition precedent to attract the vicarious liability of others.

Thus, the words "as well as the company" appearing in the Section make it absolutely unmistakably clear that when the company can be prosecuted, then only the persons mentioned in the other categories could be vicariously liable for the offence subject to the averments in the petition and proof thereof.
One cannot be oblivious of the fact that the company is a juristic person and it has its own respectability.
If a finding is recorded against it, it would create a concavity in its reputation.
There can be situations when the corporate reputation is affected when a director is indicted.

In view of our aforesaid analysis, we arrive at the irresistible conclusion that for maintaining the prosecution under Section 141 of the Act, arraigning GAC, J of a company as an accused is imperative.
The other categories of offenders can only be brought in the dragnet on the touchstone of vicarious liability as the same has been stipulated in the provision itself.
We say so on the basis of the ratio laid down in C.V. Parekh (supra) which is a three-Judge Bench decision.
Thus, the view expressed in Sheoratan Agarwal (supra) does not correctly lay down the law and, accordingly, is hereby overruled.
The decision in Anil Hada (supra) is overruled with the qualifier as stated in paragraph.
The decision in Modi Distilleries (supra) has to be treated to be restricted to its own facts as has been explained by us hereinabove."

(2) In Himanshu v. B. Shivamurthy and another2,

sentences.text: This Court held that Section 141 of the NI Act dealing with offences by companies contemplates that every person who at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

This Court,
considering the said provision, held as under:
"38.
From the aforesaid pronouncements, the principle that can be culled out is that it is the bounden duty of the court to ascertain for what purpose the legal fiction has been created.
It is also the duty of the court to imagine the fiction with all real consequences and instances unless prohibited from doing so.
That apart, the use of the term "deemed" has to be read in its context and further, the fullest logical purpose and import are to be understood.
It is because in modern legislation, the term "deemed" has been used for manifold purposes.
The object of the legislature has to be kept in mind.
xx xx xx 56.

We have referred to the aforesaid passages only to highlight that there has to be strict observance of the provisions regard being had to the legislative intendment because it deals with penal provisions and a penalty is not to be imposed affecting the rights of persons, whether juristic entities or individuals, unless they are arrayed as accused.
It is to be kept in mind that the power of punishment is vested in the GAC, J legislature and that is absolute in Section 141 of the Act which clearly speaks of commission of offence by the company.

The learned counsel for the respondents have vehemently urged that the use of the term "as well as" in the section is of immense significance and, in its tentacle, it brings in the company as well as the Director Dr.D.Bhaskara Rao, Hyd Dt., vs State Of Telangana, Rep Pp And Anr., on 5 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/192001512/
5 and/or other officers who are responsible for the acts of the company and, therefore,
a prosecution against the Directors or other officers is tenable even if the company is not arraigned as an accused.
The words "as well as" have to be understood in the context.
xx xx xx (4)

In Dayle De'souza v. Government of India through Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner and another4, wherein, it is held :
"This position was again clarified and reiterated by this Court in Himanshu v. B.
Shivamurthy and Another.

sentences.text:
The relevant portion of the judgment reads thus:
"6.
The judgment of the High Court has been questioned on two grounds.
The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that firstly, the appellant could not be prosecuted without the company being named as an accused.
The cheque was issued by the company and was signed by the appellant as its Director.
Secondly, it was urged that the observation of the High Court that the company can now be proceeded against in the complaint is misconceived.
The learned counsel submitted that the offence under Section 138 is complete only upon the issuance of a notice of demand and the failure of payment within the prescribed period.

In absence of compliance with the requirements of Section 138, it is 2021 SCC OnLine SC 1012 GAC, J asserted, the direction of the High Court that the company could be impleaded/arraigned at this stage is erroneous.
7. The first submission on behalf of the appellant is no longer res integra.

A decision of a three-Judge Bench of this Court in Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels & Tours (P)
Ltd. governs the area of dispute.

sentences.text: The issue which fell for consideration was whether an authorised signatory of a company would be liable for prosecution under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 without the company being arraigned as an accused.

Applying the same proposition of law as laid down in Aneeta Hada (supra), this Court in Hindustan Unilever Limited v. State of Madhya Pradesh applying pari materia provision in Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, held that:
"23. Clause (a) of sub-section (1) of Section 17 of the Act makes the person nominated to be in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of business and the company shall be guilty of the offences under clause (b) of sub-section (1) of Section 17 of the Act.

entities.text: Hindustan Unilever Limited v. State of Madhya Pradesh
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Therefore, there is no material distinction between Section 141 of the NI Act and Section 17 of the Act which makes the company as well as the nominated person to be held guilty of the offences and/or liable to be proceeded and punished accordingly.
Clauses (a) and (b) are not in the alternative but conjoint.
Therefore, in the absence of Criminal Appeal a/o. SLP (Crl.) No. 3913 of 2020 the company, the nominated person cannot be convicted or vice versa.

Since the Company was not convicted by the trial court, we find that the finding of the High Court to revisit the Dr.D.Bhaskara Rao, Hyd Dt., vs State Of Telangana, Rep Pp And Anr., on 5 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/192001512/
6 judgment will be unfair to the appellant-nominated person who has been facing GAC,
J trial for more than last 30 years.

sentences.text: Therefore, the order of remand to the trial court to fill up the lacuna is not a fair option exercised by the High Court as the failure of the trial court to convict the Company renders the entire conviction of the nominated person as unsustainable."
In terms of the ratio above, a company being a juristic person cannot be imprisoned, but it can be subjected to a fine, which in itself is a punishment.

Every punishment has adverse consequences,
and therefore, prosecution of the company is mandatory.
The exception would possibly be when the company itself has ceased to exist or cannot be prosecuted due to a statutory bar.
However, such exceptions are of no relevance in the present case.
Thus, the present prosecution must fail for this reason as well."
The above judgments support the case of the petitioner in the present case.
12. A detailed counter was filed by respondent No.2 with the same set of facts stated supra.

It is the specific contention of respondent No.2 that it is not a fit case to quash the proceedings, as the accused did not possess valid drug licence for KIMS IP pharmacy situated in Block-III of 11th floor as on the date of seizure of drugs i.e. 21.04.2015 and that the licence was obtained thereafter, which was valid from 12.05.2015 to 11.05.2020.

It is the specific contention of the Drug Inspector that the samples GAC, J which were being sent to the Analyst though revealed of standard quality, there is no valid licence for storing or selling those drugs in Block-III, though there is licence to sell the drugs in the pharmacy, and therefore, prayed to dismiss the petition.

13. In support of his contentions, the learned counsel for respondent No.2 has relied on the judgment in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Purshotam Dass Jhunjunwala and others5, wherein,
it is held:
"In the instant case, a clear averment has been made regarding the active role played by the respondents and the extent of their liability.

sentences.text: In this view of the matter, it cannot be said that para 5 of the complaint is vague and does not implicate respondents 1 to 11.
As to what would be the evidence against the respondents is not a matter to be considered at this stage and would have to be proved at the trial.
We have already held that for the purpose of quashing the proceedings only the allegations set forth in the complaint have to be seen and nothing further.

From a perusal of the various clauses of the complaint, including para 5, it is quite clear that a prima facie case for summoning the accused has been made out and the High Court was absolutely wrong in holding that the allegations made in para 'S' are vague.
The High Court failed to consider that the allegations were quite clear and explicit so as to be 1983 AIR 158 GAC, J sufficient for taking cognizance of the offence against the accused."
The above judgment is not applicable to the facts of the present case.

sentences.text: As far as Corporate hospitals or private hospitals are concerned, the procedure for supplying drugs is to be discussed.
Whenever a patient is admitted in hospital as inpatient and is being diagnosed by the team of Doctors of different departments, each Doctor prescribes medicines in the case sheet.

On such prescription of any medicine to the patient, it is the duty of the nursing station to keep indent to the pharmacy which is present in the hospital, in order to supply medicine to the nursing station, who in turn, will administer medicine to the patient as per the timings prescribed by the concerned Doctor.
In the present case also, the medicines were seized from the nursing station and not from the pharmacy and the said nursing station is within the premises of the hospital.
Further, the pharmacy is having licence to store as well GAC, J as to sell medicine.

The 2nd respondent/Drug Inspector has seized the medicines from the nursing station of Block-III of KIMS hospital from 3rd, 5th and 11th floors, who insisted for licence to store the drugs at the said places.
It is not the complaint of respondent No.2 that the medicines are being kept for sale at those particular places or points where the drugs were kept.

All the places where the drugs were found by the 2nd respondent, are the nursing stations in the said floor i.e. 11th floor of Block-III, where 80 types of medicines were found stored in the iron racks.
There is no evidence on record that these medicines were kept for sale as it is a nursing station.

Admittedly, KIMS hospital pharmacy has valid licence as on the date of inspection and the pharmacist has given her explanation stating that these products were kept in the nursing station in order to administer them on the patients who are on those floors i.e. 3rd, 5th and 11th floors of the hospital.
Therefore, this Court is of the considered view that these drugs were stored only for the purpose of administering to the inpatients and not for sale.

If at all those drugs were kept for sale, the 2nd respondent ought to have seized some other material such as the GAC, J medical prescriptions, bills for the medicines already sold by the nursing station at relevant point of time and also blank bill books and receipts from the said places.
In the absence of these documents being seized from the said places, those places where the drugs are stored by the hospital authorities, cannot be presumed to be stored for sale.

Admittedly, none of the patients nor their attendants have made any complaint against the KIMS hospital authorities that they are selling the medicines at particular points, from where the 2nd respondent has seized the medicines.
The complaint itself shows that on credible information, they have visited the place, but who has given such information, is not known.
Even the complaint does not disclose that they have received an anonymous information that sale of medicines is being done at the KIMS hospital at different places.
Admittedly, all the 80 kinds of drugs are stored in iron racks in the nursing station of KIMS hospital.
Therefore, this Court holds that it is a fit case to quash the proceedings against the petitioner, who is the Managing Director of the KIMS hospital.
GAC, J 16.

sentences.text: Admittedly, the seizure was made on 21.04.2015, which pertains to 11th floor and this licence was being taken at the instance of 2nd respondent as they insisted them to take for each and every place where the drugs were being stored.
The reply also discloses that the drugs were taken for the purpose of administering GAC, J to the inpatients according to the pharmacy receipts and the said receipts were also seized.

The pharmacy receipts are also enclosed along with the quash petition,
which clearly show that they were purchased for the purpose of administering to inpatients viz.,
Rukmini Bai, Hanumantha Reddy, Venkateshwara Raju, Gopichand, Chenna Kristaiah, Sarma KVK,
Lingamma, Ramu Yadav, Sundari, Rajamalla Reddy, Ahemad S.J., etc.,
which are annexed along with the case sheets from Page Nos.118 to 294 of the quash petition.

Therefore, it can be construed that the medicines which were purchased from the KIMS Pharma were stored at the respective nursing stations of the hospital in order to administer them to the inpatients.
In the absence of any alleged crime, innocents cannot be tried.

In view of the same, it is a fit case to quash the proceedings against the petitioner/ Managing Director of KIMS hospital.
20.

Accordingly, this petition is allowed and the proceedings initiated against the petitioner in C.C.No.2267 of 2015 on the file of XI Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate at Secunderabad,
Hyderabad District, are hereby quashed.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Applying the doctrine of strict construction, we are of the considered opinion that commission of offence by the company is an express condition precedent to attract the vicarious liability of others.
In view of our aforesaid analysis, we arrive at the irresistible conclusion that for maintaining the prosecution under Section 141 of the Act, arraigning GAC, J of a company as an accused is imperative.
(2) In Himanshu v. B. Shivamurthy and another2,
Dr.D.Bhaskara Rao, Hyd Dt., vs State Of Telangana, Rep Pp And Anr., on 5 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/192001512/
4 wherein, it is held:
"In the absence of the company being arraigned as an accused, a complaint against the appellant was therefore not maintainable.
(3) In Hindustan Unilever Limited v. State of Madhya Pradesh3, wherein, it is held;
(2019) 3 SCC 797 (2020) 10 SCC 751 GAC, J "A three-Judge Bench of this Court in Aneeta Hada v.
Godfather Travels & Tours Private Limited11 considered the question of conviction of the Directors in the absence of the Company in proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act,
1881 as also in the proceedings under Information Technology Act, 2000.
The object of the legislature has to be kept in mind.
xx xx xx 56.
We have referred to the aforesaid passages only to highlight that there has to be strict observance of the provisions regard being had to the legislative intendment because it deals with penal provisions and a penalty is not to be imposed affecting the rights of persons, whether juristic entities or individuals, unless they are arrayed as accused.
It is to be kept in mind that the power of punishment is vested in the GAC, J legislature and that is absolute in Section 141 of the Act which clearly speaks of commission of offence by the company.
In Dayle De'souza v. Government of India through Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner and another4, wherein, it is held :
"This position was again clarified and reiterated by this Court in Himanshu v. B.
Shivamurthy and Another.
A decision of a three-Judge Bench of this Court in Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels & Tours (P)
Ltd. governs the area of dispute.
Since the Company was not convicted by the trial court, we find that the finding of the High Court to revisit the Dr.D.Bhaskara Rao, Hyd Dt., vs State Of Telangana, Rep Pp And Anr., on 5 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/192001512/
6 judgment will be unfair to the appellant-nominated person who has been facing GAC,
J trial for more than last 30 years.
It is not the complaint of respondent No.2 that the medicines are being kept for sale at those particular places or points where the drugs were kept.
If at all those drugs were kept for sale, the 2nd respondent ought to have seized some other material such as the GAC, J medical prescriptions, bills for the medicines already sold by the nursing station at relevant point of time and also blank bill books and receipts from the said places.
In the absence of these documents being seized from the said places, those places where the drugs are stored by the hospital authorities, cannot be presumed to be stored for sale.
But, in the present case, drugs were not stored for selling them, but they were stored for administering to the inpatients in the hospital.
Therefore, this Court finds no error or irregularity committed by the petitioner/accused.
Therefore, it can be construed that the medicines which were purchased from the KIMS Pharma were stored at the respective nursing stations of the hospital in order to administer them to the inpatients.
